title: Theremins: World's First Electronic Music
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the theremin, the world's first electronic musical instrument, invented by Lev Sergeyevich Termen (Leon Theremin) in early 1920s Russia while he was trying to build a proximity sensor. They cover his promotion tours for Lenin and the Soviet state, his spying, his years in New York and the RCA theremin, his gulag and sharashka imprisonment, the Great Seal Bug, his later neglect and return to public view, the theremin's use in film and pop/psychedelic music (Samuel Hoffman, Robert Moog, Beach Boys' electro-theremin, Star Trek theme myth), how the instrument works (two antennas, pitch and volume, body capacitance), and how hard it is to play, with Clara Rockmore and Toby, plus a listener mail segment about a book purchase for a stranger through the Stuff You Should Know Army.

segments.title: Opening banter and describing the theremin
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter, then describe the theremin's eerie sound, its hand-controlled electromagnetic operation, and collect hapless listener-style descriptions of its sound.

segments.title: Invention by Termen and Lenin's tour
segments.summary: Lev Termen, a young physicist at the Physical Technical Institute in St. Petersburg, was developing a proximity sensor when he added sound and realized it could be musical. Lenin backed a tour promoting electricity and the instrument across Russia and Western Europe.

segments.title: Espionage, New York years and RCA theremin
segments.summary: During his European tours Termen spied for the Soviet state. He lived in New York for about a decade, married Lavinia Williams, and RCA bought rights and sold a theremin for about 175 dollars, which sold poorly.

segments.title: Return to USSR, gulag and sharashka
segments.summary: Termen left the US in 1938 in debt and without telling his wife. He was imprisoned in the gulag and later moved to a sharashka science prison where he developed new devices.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before returning.

segments.title: The Great Seal Bug and the Barn
segments.summary: Termen invented the Buran listening device and the Great Seal Bug, a passive wooden bug hidden in a carved Great Seal given to Ambassador Averell Harriman in Moscow, activated by microwaves and discovered by a British radio operator after about seven years.

segments.title: Later life, neglect and legacy in film
segments.summary: A 1967 New York Times article by Harold Schonberg found Termen at the Moscow Conservatory, after which the Soviets ruined his career. He lived in poverty until the 1980s, then moved to Europe and the US. The theremin was used in 1940s films like Spellbound and The Lost Weekend.

segments.title: Theremin in pop, lounge and psychedelic music
segments.summary: Samuel Hoffman and Miklos Rozsa popularized the theremin in lounge and exotica. Robert Moog sold theremin kits. Rolling Stones, Led Zeppelin, and others used it. The Beach Boys' Good Vibrations features an electro-theremin by Paul Tanner, not a true theremin, and the Star Trek theme does not use one.

segments.title: Theremin in film and later bands
segments.summary: The hosts mention theremin appearances in Tim Burton films, Hellboy, First Man, and bands like Mercury Rev, Silver Apples, and Lothar and the Hand People.

segments.title: How the theremin works and how to play it
segments.summary: The theremin has two antennas: a vertical one controlling pitch and a horizontal loop controlling volume. Two oscillators interact with the player's body capacitance to produce the sound. Playing requires a good ear and precise, still hand movements, as described by Clara Rockmore.

segments.title: Modern theremins and Toby
segments.summary: Modern theremins such as Moog's models offer chord recognition and adjustable forgiveness. The hosts mention DIY kits and Toby, a Dallas theremin player who joined the Polyphonic Spree. Descendants Natasha and Peter Theremin are noted.

segments.title: Listener mail: book gift via Stuff You Should Know Army
segments.summary: A listener named Richard Roberts describes how Army members bought a copy of the Stuff You Should Know book for a stranger who found it at her library. Jacko du Bois is thanked.
